segments.text: A Few-Shot Contrastive Learning Framework for Industrial Dataset Cleaning Using Cross-Domain Embedding Optimization Abstract- The accuracy of computer vision models across various applications in industry and environment is severely compromised by dataset noise and class imbalance. However, existing cleaning frameworks are not suitable for limited-label scenarios, where datasets gathered from heterogeneous sources have inconsistent visual quality. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new algorithm—IndusCleanNet, a few-shot dataset cleaning mechanism based on supervised contrastive learning and cross-domain embedding optimization. The model operates in two stages: the first stage uses an EfficientNet backbone pre-trained with contrastive loss on the NEU Surface Defect Dataset to enhance texture and structural cues and the second stage uses prototype-based clustering and embedding distance regularization to identify defective, irrelevant, or redundant samples through few-shot fine-tuning. The final cleaning decision is made by a lightweight attention-guided autoencoder ensemble that limits feature redundancy and improves anomaly detection precision. Our experimental results show that IndusCleanNet obtains a 96.84% cleaning accuracy that is higher by 5.71% compared to the original contrastive cleaner and improves defect classification by 17.92% over unfiltered datasets. These results validate the algorithm’s efficacy in maintaining data integrity while significantly improving downstream prediction reliability. The proposed method thus establishes a robust, domain-independent cleaning mechanism applicable to large-scale industrial vision datasets and other non-medical imaging tasks. Keywords: Few-shot learning; Contrastive learning; Dataset cleaning; Industrial defect detection; EfficientNet; Cross-domain adaptation. I Introduction The performance of data-driven industrial systems is often limited by the integrity and relevance of visual datasets when it comes to successful defect detection, anomaly recognition, and predictive maintenance [1]. When working with industrial image corpora, poor lighting conditions, class frequencies, and sensor-related noises affect the generalization capabilities of any model [2][3]. Furthermore, the multi-sensor and multi environment-based data are more likely to produce too many redundant or irrelevant samples that only increase the difficulty of obtaining an optimal training model [4][5]. Moreover, in many life systems and manufacturing as well as inspection plants, there is an excess of unlabeled or poorly labeled data that is generated regularly. Considering that data annotation severely lacks both economically and temporally, several low-supervision, automated methods for data preparation are urgently required [6]. The existing applied techniques are ineffective for life system data since the statistical and clustering-oriented cleaning methods fail to capture the texture dependencies and defect-related clues [7]. It leads to a growing tendency to use a
segments.label: human

segments.text: learning-oriented approach that not only generalizes well cross-data types but also adapts effectively to the few -shot learning settings due to data sparsity [8]. Few-shot learning has emerged as a prominent paradigm in the recent past for handling rigid data conditions through the integration of meta-learning and contrastive optimization principles [9][10]. It has critical applications in the broader field of industrial vision as visual errors often emanate from microscopic changes in the material texture, slight variance in lighting in different capture settings, and changes in operations. Contrastive learning enables models to generate discriminative, domain invariant embeddings by pushing dissimilar samples apart and pulling those from the same category together [11]. However, the model’s capacity to learn quality embeddings as determined by the stability of the output is significantly compromised in industrial datasets due to varying defect morphologies. The use of few-shot techniques in the contrastive embeddings sub-field is especially challenging when used to refine the embedding results in error as the work scope expands to eliminate irrelevant images; thus, the current work is severely undermined in this regard. These issues necessitate a model capable of learning stable, refined embeddings by aligning the embeddings from the different domains into a single space to achieve intra-class compactness and inter-class separability [12]. We present IndusCleanNet, a few-shot contrastive learning framework for industrial dataset cleaning in low-labeled and cross-domain scenarios [13][14]. IndusCleanNet utilizes a pre-trained EfficientNet backbone also on the NEU Surface Defect Dataset, allowing the model to capture fine textural details of industrial defects. It leverages a two-stage pipeline, where the model first approaches supervised contrastive loss to learn discriminative embeddings before few-shot fine-tuning to minimize embedding distances between clean samples and noisy samples [15][16]. Prototype-based clustering is designed to separate the defective, irrelevant, and noisy samples while embedding regularization boosts the adaptation’s stability. An attention-guided autoencoder ensemble enhances decision trustworthiness by post-cleaning outputs, removing feature redundancy, and boosting anomaly sensitivity [17]. The combined use of representation learning, clustering intelligence, and attention-based feature reconstruction provides a robust, consistent, and domain-agnostic cleaning strategy for industrial visual data represented. For reasons, this paper is inspired by the need to improve the quality of data for succeeding industrial vision tasks, given the role of training data fidelities in the reliability of predictions and system vagility [18]. While qualified and balanced data improve the rate of convergence, it also enhances robust decision in the presence of operational variances in the real-world [19], [15]. The following three specific industrial data challenges; namely, the heterogeneous noise, class imbalance, and domain inconsistency are uniquely addressed by IndusCleanNet. The learning-based architect balances both the feature representation and the data integrity by binding few-shot adaptability with cross-domain contrastive learning [20]. An explicit improvement in data quality and accuracy of defect classification are observed. These results prove that cleaning through intelligent embedding refinement represents a sustainable strategy for safeguarding the model’s reliability and boosting its interpretability in the

In summary, the contributions of the paper are as follows: 1) IndusCleanNet: introduces a few-shot dataset cleaner, IndusCleanNet, with a supervised contrastive learning and cross-domain embedding optimisation framework to clean the noisy, redundant, and irrelevant data samples from them. 2) Attention-Guided Autoencoder Ensemble: Introduces a lightweight ensemble of attention-based autoencoders to improve the cleaning results by dissecting the feature redundancy and improving anomaly detection sensitivity. 3) Cross-domain performance: Proves robust performance across industrial datasets, demonstrating that the proposed model maintains data integrity and improves the accuracy of defect classifications in the case of limited patterns. The rest of the paper is organized as the following sections: the Related Works section provides an extensive overview of the few-shot and contrastive frameworks in cleaning and the overall capacity of few-shot learning from an industrial perspective. The Methodology section explains the architecture of IndusCleanNet, with the description of the dual-stage design, prototype clustering, and attention-based ensemble. The Experimental Analysis section details dataset configuration, metrics calculated, and the ablation analysis that proves the effectiveness of the proposed framework. The Results and Analysis section reviews the outcomes of the experiments and compares these with the baselines. The Conclusion section summarises the implications of the paper in the realm of industrial artificial intelligence and presents wide-scope potential future directions. segments.text: Figure 1: Overall Architecture of IndusCleanNet – Contrastive Pretraining and Few-Shot Fine-Tuning Framework 3.1 Data Acquisition The NEU Surface Defect Database was deliberately chosen as a benchmark for the Selection of CNN-Based Clustering Core of the IndusCleanNet Framework. I chose this dataset due to its rich representation of real-world industrial problems, specifically in the area of metal surface defect detection. In the metal surface defect detection area, data inconsistency such as variance in image capturing conditions and natural variation such contrast, roughness, and illumination, in addition to texture complexity, occurred more frequently in images. The NEU-CLS dataset also provides the ideal platform to train and evaluate the dataset cleaning algorithms. These images are actually surface images taken under various conditions of roughness, contrasts, and illuminations which are all types of intrinsic noises likely to occur during production. The NEU-CPS dataset strikes a balance between the ideal situation of a laboratory environment and natural variation, guaranteeing that the model will be faced with the same kind of noises that are present where manufacturing plants are. Furthermore, the dataset’s availability through Kaggle (https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/kaustubhdikshit/neu-surface-defect-database) provides transparency, reproducibility, and accessibility—qualities essential for a robust academic study. In addition to the above reasons, the choice of using the NEU-CLS database from other larger commercial datasets or proprietary datasets is also due to its moderate size, which makes it suitable for few-shot learning paradigms. Specifically, NEU-CLS allows simulating limited-labeled industrial under few-shot setups efficiently, as annotating large-scale datasets is often time-consuming and labor-intensive. Hence, by utilizing NEU-CLS the current study maintains methodological relevance, computational viability, and domain adaptiveness – which are all crucial to prove the generalization ability of IndusCleanNet in practical industrial settings. The NEU Surface Defect Database consists of 1,800 grayscale images with a size of 200 × 200 pixels each and includes six unique classes of steel surface defects:
segments.label: human

segments.text: crazing, inclusion, patches, pitted surface, rolled-in scale, and scratches. Each defect category includes 300 images, and hence, the class distribution is balanced and feasible for both supervised and contrastive learning setup. For the experiments, the dataset was distributed into 70% training 1,260 images, 20% validation 360 images, and 10% testing 180 images subsets. While the training images were used for the pretraining of the EfficientNet backbone contrastively, the validation set was employed for hyperparameter tuning and the optimization of the embedded space. No testing subset was used until the end of the evaluation to ensure an unbiased performance assessment. The testing subset was reserved only for the final evaluation to maintain unbiased performance assessment. All the images in each dataset underwent preprocessing such as grayscale normalization, Gaussian noise filtering, and pixel intensity standardization to eliminate imaging acquisition artifacts and enhance visual similarity. Therefore, this well-structured image data preparation setup maintains the intrinsic visual of different defect types while removing unnecessary noise, which helps IndusCleanNet to distinguish features at the level of texture while aligning the domain. Therefore, NEU-CLS maintains consistent labeling and visual similarity and can be utilized as a solid benchmark for demonstrating the ability of data cleaning or representation learning models in industrial data classification tasks. 3.2 Data Preprocessing and Noise Characterization Raw data in industrial image datasets often suffer from variations in illumination, surface reflectivity, and noise introduced by imaging sensors or environmental conditions. EfficientNet-B0 was employed as the backbone in this stage, where the compound scaling technique was levied, ensuring that the network depth, width, and resolution are uniformly balanced to achieve superiority along with nominal computational expense. The pretrained ImageNet weights were used to initialize the backbone to provide generalized low-level filter state for edge and structure recognition, which was ultimately updated through supervised contrastive learning. The main goal of this phase is to develop an embedding space in which the samples of the same defect category are closely clattered, and at the same time, they are separated from the other class samples via a considerable margin. This structure-aware learning approach is imperative in the industrial domain as, in many cases, the differences in the appearance and visual characteristics between the defect are subtle, and acquiring such fine-grained interclass changes by utilizing the traditional cross-entropy training regime is not possible. Hence, the network does not merely synthesize a feature to classify but to know the relationship structure between the surface pattern. Due to dissimilarity in surface reflectivity, imaging angles, and texture noise, the domain shift exhibited in industrial defect datasets cannot be addressed through conventional retraining. Hence, we adopt an adaptation paradigm known as few-shot learning wherein we employ a scanty number of annotated samples, typically between 3 and 5 per defect class, to re- calibrate the learned feature space. In daily industrial practice, new data from different production lines or distinguished visual environments render the learned model non-generalizable over the target hardware, causing the feature responses to be unstable and the performance to degrade. To take it into account, a domain-invariant feature alignment technique is incorporated via Maximum Mean Discrepancy -based optimization. The MMD approach minimizes the distributional distance between source embeddings and target embeddings within a reproducing kernel Hilbert 𝑍𝑠 𝑍𝑡 space (RKHS). The MMD loss is mathematically expressed as in Eq.11: ​ ​ ​ (11) 𝐿𝑀𝑀𝐷= 1 𝑛𝑠𝑖=1 𝑛𝑠 ∑ϕ 𝑧𝑖 𝑠 ( ) − 1 𝑛𝑡𝑗=1 𝑛𝑡 ∑ϕ 𝑧𝑗 𝑡 ( ) |||| |||| |||| ||||𝐻 2 Where represents a kernel-induced mapping and is the associated Hilbert space. By ϕ ·( ) 𝐻 minimizing this loss, the model is encouraged to align high-order statistics between the two domains, driving down the discrepancy in embedding distributions and learning model structure consistency. This aligns the pretrained EfficientNet and fine-tuned prototype clusters to novel datasets in one-stop shopping without the full retraining. Besides, the MMD constraint can be seen as a distribution regularizer that encourages a smoother embedding manifold in which source and target features cohabit the same latent subspace. The learned texture and pattern descriptors can be more general, allowing for recognition of new surface anomalies under varying illumination conditions, noise levels, sensor equipment, etc. . Moreover, a gradient reversal layer is implemented to enhance domain invariance in an adversarial training framework. The GRL enables feature adaptation with a corrective action by endorsing the feature extractor to a domain discriminator in an aggressive optimization process. The 𝐹 𝐷 discriminator seeks to classify whether a feature originates from the source domain or the target domain, and the feature extractor is trained to fool the discriminator, leading to domain-agnostic feature extraction. Consequently, the update direction for the feature extractor was reversed, which guaranteed that the learned embeddings would be chosen in such a way that the discriminability between domains should be minimized. The experiment was conducted in a workstation with an NVIDIA RTX 4090 24 GB VRAM GPU and powered by an Intel Core i9 processor with 64 GB RAM. The experimental environment was developed in Python 3.10 leveraging the Tensorflow and Pytorch backends. The source data for this study was the NEU Surface Defect dataset, preprocessed, and split into 70%, 15% validation, and 15% test data to balance its proportional distribution relative to the frequency per class. The input samples used in the study were resized to pixels and 224×224 rescaled to the range [0,1]. The training set employed data augmentations like random cropping, horizontal flipping, Gaussian blurring, etc. to introduce visual disruption to artificial industrial vectors and promote visual dissimilarity among the samples. The training process was executed with a batch size of 32, optimized with the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of decaying exponentially after each epoch. Three separate 1 × 10 −4

segments.text: training sessions were to be conducted for each parameter set replaced to mitigate variations in performance metric. 4.2 Experimental Setup The experimentation setup consisted of a dual evaluation pipeline, focusing on the precision of data cleansing and downstream defect classification improvement. In the first phase, the model was prescreened with supervised contrastive loss on the NEU dataset to detect domain-agnostic embedding properties. In the second phase, overseen with prototype clustering on few-shot fine-tuning of small labeled samples, in line with the sparse labeling of industrial applications. Maximum Mean Discrepancy and gradient reversal methods aligned cross-domain embeddings to ensure contradictions did not arise due to the inability of the model to stabilize distinct features. An attention supervised autoencoder was used to refine the final screening output by inspecting the reconstruction loss, the decreased term in entropy, and the attention weight excerpt. The overall experimental definition was configured to gauge the ability of IndusCleanNet to separate redundant and erratic samples from the mislabeling from meaningful visual-texture similarities in inter-class defect distributions. segments.text: Therefore, the obtained results prove the importance of data-cleaning integrity for predictive dependability in industrial vision. 5.1 Ablation Study Finally, the contribution of each module to the proposed IndusCleanNet architecture was examined in an ablation study. Under the same clustering and few-shot learning settings, the ablation study progressively ablated critical components: Contrastive pretraining, prototype clustering, and cross-domain optimization: Figure 1 shows the results. Excluding contrastive pretraining reduced the cleaning accuracy to 91.13%, indicating that the process is critical in learning the ability to differentiate defective patterns in textures from industrial surfaces. Omitting prototype clustering reduced the cleaning accuracy to 93.20%; thus, the module is sufficient in tuning inter-class relationships within few-shot learning assumptions. Omitting cross-domain embedding optimization reduced the cleaning accuracy to 94.50%; the findings suggest that the process is adequate for aligning features into a stable representation across dissimilar domains. The cleaning accuracy was highest when all modules were integrated, the IndusCleanNet, with a cleaning accuracy of 96.84%, showing that the combined effect of the three modules minimizes noise, enhances intra-class consistency, and promotes stable domain adaptation during industrial dataset cleaning. segments.text: 5.2 Discussion Overall, the experimental results support the above claims and show the advanced model capability and generalization of IndusCleanNet in industrial dataset cleaning and downstream defect classification. Concretely, it would obtain the highest accuracy and feature purity in the performance comparison with existing models. This result proves the strength and the effectiveness of the hybrid architecture that combined the contrastive pretraining, the prototype-based clustering, and domain alignment, which we have also verified that the later one makes the dataset more generalizable for the training process to reduce the influence of the mislabel and the noise data. The increased accuracy rate in the defect classification further shows the correlation between the data purification process and the learning model. Ultimately, IndusCleanNet is an easily distributed and an efficient solution to industrial data intelligence that paves the way to high-integrity machine learning in manufacturing. VI Conclusion In conclusion, the proposed IndusCleanNet achieved remarkable results with 96.84% of cleaning accuracy, F1-score of 0.96%, and 0.90% feature purity ratio, thus outperforming the current models in industrial dataset cleaning. By combining contrastive pretraining, prototype-based clustering, and cross-domain embedding optimization, the model could effectively reduce noise, improve data quality, and enhance the performance of downstream defect classification by 17.92%. Overall, these results prove the robustness and generalizability of all the proposed frameworks across different domains heterogeneity thus establishing IndusCleanNet as an efficient few shot learning cleaning framework. The future work of this model includes extension to multi-modality datasets, including temporal defect learning, and self-supervised adaptation to continue the operational performance in evolving industrial environments.
